content.title: About
content.content: Chickpeas (Cicer arietinum) are a legume native to the Mediterranean, South Asia and North Africa. The seeds have a nutty flavor, firm texture and are used whole, as flour, in hummus and in a wide range of dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chickpeas belong to the legume family and have been cultivated for over 7,000 years.
In India they are called “garbanzo” or “chana”, while in the Mediterranean they are often referred to as “Egyptian peas”.
The plant can fix atmospheric nitrogen, enriching the soil.
Chickpeas are a staple in vegetarian and vegan diets as a plant‑based protein source.
More than 50 varieties exist, differing in size, color and flavor.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas provide about 20 % protein, making them a valuable amino‑acid source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of iron and folate
items.content: Iron aids oxygen transport, while folate is essential for cell division and fetal development.

items.title: Contains magnesium and phosphorus
items.content: These minerals contribute to muscle function, nerve health and bone formation.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Chickpeas raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chickpeas, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or sprouting helps mitigate this.

items.title: Gas production
items.content: Legumes can cause increased gas in sensitive people.

items.title: Potential gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: People with celiac disease should choose certified gluten‑free chickpeas.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Chickpeas can be boiled, roasted, baked, ground into flour, or blended into hummus. Add them to salads, soups, stews, curries, as well as to vegetarian patties and falafel.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry chickpeas in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage keep them in the refrigerator. Cooked chickpeas keep in the fridge for 4‑5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut butter cookie is a crunchy biscuit that incorporates peanut butter into the dough. It combines the sweetness of sugar with the creamy taste of peanuts, making a popular snack suitable for both children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial production of peanut butter cookies began in the United States in the 1930s.
Peanut butter used in cookies is often natural peanut paste without added sugar or salt.
Peanut butter cookies are frequently used as a base for dessert bars and ice‑cream sandwiches.
In some countries the cookie is a traditional school snack.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 25 % protein, which helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats in peanuts support heart health.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Peanuts are a good source of iron, essential for blood formation.

items.title: Supports blood‑sugar stability
items.content: The low glycemic index of peanut butter helps keep glucose levels steady.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: People with peanut allergy may experience severe reactions when consuming the cookie.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The fat content makes the cookie energy‑dense, so portion control is advised.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions can contribute to tooth decay and metabolic issues.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Some brands add salt and preservatives, which may be undesirable for those with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peanut butter cookies can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, crumbled into yogurt or ice cream, or used in dessert recipes such as cakes and cheesecakes. For children, choose varieties without added sugar or excess salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cookies in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep them in the refrigerator to prevent the fats from becoming rancid.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-poult.title: Whole‑grain Pasta with Cream Sauce, Poultry and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Whole‑grain pasta with a cream sauce, poultry (such as chicken, turkey or duck) and added vegetables is a balanced dish that combines complex carbohydrates, protein and fiber. The whole‑grain pasta retains the bran and germ, providing B‑vitamins, iron and magnesium. The cream sauce is usually made from cream or low‑fat milk, while the vegetables (e.g., broccoli, carrot, bell pepper) add vitamins, minerals and antioxidants.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta has a lower glycemic index than regular white pasta, helping to keep you fuller longer.
Cream sauces can be enriched with plant oils to reduce saturated fat without sacrificing flavor.
The poultry used is often chicken, but turkey or duck can be used, changing the amino‑acid profile.
Adding vegetables to the sauce raises the fiber content to about 5–7 g per serving.
The tradition of pairing pasta with cream sauce began in Italy in the early 1920s, but the whole‑grain and vegetable version became popular in the 2000s.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Poultry adds high‑quality protein needed for muscle repair and immune function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole grains contain thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Broccoli, carrots and bell peppers are rich in vitamin C, beta‑carotene and other phytochemicals that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D in the sauce
items.content: When the cream sauce is dairy‑based, it contributes calcium and vitamin D, important for bone health.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Cream sauce and pasta can make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Lactose presence
items.content: Dairy‑based cream sauce contains lactose, which may be problematic for lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain added salt; choose low‑sodium versions or make the sauce at home.

items.title: Wheat allergy / gluten
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta contains gluten; people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should use gluten‑free alternatives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the cream sauce, pieces of cooked poultry and vegetables. Garnish with fresh herbs (basil, parsley) and a sprinkle of grated Parmesan. For a lighter version, use reduced‑fat cream or plant‑based milk alternatives.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Cream sauce may separate; gently reheat and stir before serving. Keep dry whole‑grain pasta in a cool, dry place in a sealed package.

content.title: About
content.content: Pina Colada is a ready‑to‑drink cocktail mix based on pineapple juice, coconut cream, and rum (non‑alcoholic version without rum). It has a sweet tropical flavor, creamy texture, and a strong aroma of pineapple and coconut.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pina Colada was officially declared the national drink of Puerto Rico in 1978.
The first recipe appeared in the 1950s at the Caribe Hilton bar in San Juan.
A non‑alcoholic version is widely used in kids' menus and venues where alcohol is prohibited.
The mixture can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 7 days without losing flavor or aroma.
Pina Colada is often served in a highball glass with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Pineapple juice is rich in vitamin C, which supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Coconut cream provides potassium, important for fluid balance and muscle function.

items.title: Quick Energy
items.content: Sugars from pineapple and coconut give a fast source of glucose for an energy boost.

items.title: Bromelain
items.content: Pineapple contains the enzyme bromelain, which aids digestion and reduces inflammation.

items.title: Hydration Support
items.content: The water content in the juice and coconut cream helps maintain body hydration.

items.title: High Sugar Content
items.content: The sweet taste comes from added sugars, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Coconut Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to coconut cream.

items.title: Caloric Density
items.content: Coconut cream and pineapple juice make the drink relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Alcohol Content in Traditional Recipe
items.content: Classic Pina Colada contains rum; non‑alcoholic versions omit it, but always check the label if total abstinence is required.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve Pina Colada chilled, often over ice, in a tall glass. Garnish with pineapple chunks, a cherry, or a sprinkle of toasted coconut. The non‑alcoholic version works as a refreshing summer drink and as a base for dessert cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the ready‑to‑drink mix in a sealed container in the refrigerator for no more than 5‑7 days. If frozen, sugar may crystallize; gently thaw and stir before serving.
